claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a thin, naturally formed iron-oxide surface layer.
The native oxide on pre-exposure Q235 consists primarily of Fe3O4 with minor Fe2O3.
The native oxide initially protects Q235 from corrosive species at room temperature.
Low defect density and thermodynamic stability account for the native oxide's room-temperature protection.
At 700–900 °C, thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and Q235 promotes oxide spallation.
Temperature-induced transformations of the iron oxide promote its spallation at high temperature.
The oxide's phase composition and thermal-expansion compatibility govern its integrity and interfacial adhesion.
Molten salt can dissolve portions of the oxide through formation of soluble chlorides.
Loss of the intact oxide exposes fresh Q235 metal and accelerates salt-induced corrosion.
Q235 with an intact native oxide will show minimal mass change and limited corrosion in the room-temperature salt solution.
Q235 exposed to molten salt at 700–900 °C will suffer significantly greater mass loss and corrosion damage than a protective stainless-steel reference.
High-temperature corrosion damage will include increased attack depth and microstructural degradation.
A stainless-steel reference is protected by a continuous, adherent chromia scale.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies to mild steels that depend on non-engineered native oxide scales.
The mechanism may not apply to stainless steels with enhanced passivation.
The mechanism may not apply after active surface treatment.
Comparing intact, removed, and deliberately pre-oxidized Q235 surfaces under otherwise identical exposures is proposed to isolate the role of oxide integrity.
Similar corrosion and spallation for intact and oxide-removed or modified specimens would falsify oxide spallation as the governing cause.
